newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA PETROCHEMICAL SECTOR MULLS TAIWANESE PLANT.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA PETROCHEMICAL SECTOR MULLS TAIWANESE PLANT.

text.p: The South African petrochemicals industry is seriously weighing up a Taiwanese proposal for a $3.4 billion aromatics plant in the Eastern Cape, despite serious doubts about its viability.
The industry had promised to react to the proposal by the end of September, but several key players including Polifin Ltd could not attend meetings scheduled for this week.
The meetings are now scheduled for the second week of October and plans by Taiwan to issue a press release about the project next week might have to be delayed.

The plant, which would be a joint venture project between the two countries to produce polyester fibre for the textile industry, was proposed on a recent visit to South Africa by a Taiwanese delegation led by Deputy Premier Hsu Li-Teh.
"There is hesitancy on the practicalities of the project, but it is clear that we need to show some support because the government wants this," an industry source said.
The government has identified the Coega Industrial Development Zone off Algoa Bay in the Eastern Cape for the plant, which is expected to create up to 80,000 jobs in spin-off developments.
The Eastern Cape is an African National Congress (ANC) stronghold with high levels of poverty and unemployment and the ANC is understood to be keen to stimulate development in the region.

Hsu's promises of substantial investment in South Africa have been met with some cynicism in the industry as being a ploy to win South Africa's support in the diplomatic wrangle over the "two China's" issue.
Industry sources said a major concern about the project was that it was aimed at boosting job creation in the Eastern Cape by producing polyester for a new labour intensive textile complex.
"South Africa should only consider building such a plant if it can compete with the rest of the world in textiles," an industry source said.
"That assumes that the garments made will be exported and that labour rates in the textile industry will compete with other parts of the world."

Unless the government was prepared to implement its highly contested "flexible" wage policy to get around union norms of minimum wages, which are above those in the Far East, the plant would not be a world player in exports.
The competitiveness of the plant would also be affected by the fact that the feedstock to produce the aromatics would be imported crude or naphtha.
This raised the question of whether South Africa should instead consider a plant just to meet local needs, analysts said.

A recent edition of local newspaper Engineering News said if the petrochemical complex went ahead it was likely to receive some tax benefits, including three years accelerated depreciation on assets, coupled with a two-year tax holiday.
